study_type.claude: Mixed methods (developer survey plus thematic analysis of StackOverflow threads)
study_type.nlm: Mixed methods (literature-guided survey, Likert analysis, thematic analysis, Q&A thread mining)

research_method.claude: Developer survey (11 questions, closed- and open-ended; 4-point scales analysed numerically, inductive thematic analysis) plus thematic analysis of 38 StackOverflow threads selected from 169 search results
research_method.nlm: Literature-guided survey with Likert analysis and thematic analysis, plus thematic analysis of 38 accepted StackOverflow threads
research_method.value: Literature-guided developer survey (11 questions; closed-ended 4-point agreement/frequency scales analysed by mean scores and ranks, open-ended answers by thematic analysis; 170 responses) plus thematic analysis of 38 StackOverflow threads with accepted answers (query "flaky test hasaccepted:yes")
research_method.note: '169 search results' reported only by Claude (not contradicted).

context.claude: Mixed; developers recruited via Twitter, LinkedIn and Sheffield Digital, commercial and/or open-source, no specific organization; StackOverflow community
context.nlm: Mixed (commercial and open-source software development); 170 survey respondents and 38 StackOverflow threads
context.value: mixed; developers recruited via Twitter, LinkedIn and Sheffield Digital (commercial and/or open-source development, no specific organization), plus StackOverflow threads; 170 survey respondents and 38 threads

ai_discussed.note: ML only mentioned as a domain whose random data makes tests flaky.

cat_productivity.note: Both tag the perceived productivity/efficiency-loss statements (SQ4.2, SQ4.3) as Productivity, but these are agreement ratings; perceived productivity goes to cat_survey per the definitions.

cat_quality.note: Flaky tests (test reliability), their frequency and causes are the study object.

cat_satisfaction.note: NotebookLM tags the testing-confidence-loss statement (SQ4.4) as Satisfaction/DevEx and lists frustration as a psychological cost; Claude mentions frustration only as a negative factor and tags confidence under Quality/Productivity/DevEx.

cat_activity.note: NotebookLM tags several self-reported frequency items (flaky test observation, actions, ignoring failures) as Activity, but none is repository activity.

cat_delivery.note: NotebookLM tags the perceived CI-hindrance statement (SQ4.5) as Delivery/Productivity; Claude's only Delivery tag is a literature-cited build-restart statistic (Durieux et al.).

cat_devex.note: 'Developer experience' in the title is generic; no DevEx framework.

cat_agile.note: Claude tags the self-reported action frequencies (re-run, quarantine, repair) as Process; NotebookLM tags them Activity/DevEx. CI is the context, no sprint/workflow metric.

cat_survey.note: Developer survey with 4-point agreement and frequency scales.

evidence.quote: To that end, we designed a literature-guided developer survey that we deployed on social media, receiving 170 total responses. We also searched on StackOverflow and analyzed 38 threads relevant to flaky tests, offering a distinct perspective free of any self-reporting bias.
We performed thematic analysis [11] on the questions and accepted answers in these threads to gain insights into the flaky tests for which developers require assistance to diagnose and repair.
The query we used was "flaky test hasaccepted:yes".
We disseminated the survey on Twitter and LinkedIn, specifically asking for developer participants. We also circulated the survey among Sheffield Digital, a regional technology business forum [7].
SQ10: How many years experience do you have in commercial and/or open-source software development?
To address RQ2, this question posed eight statements and asked participants to rate their agreement on a four-point scale.
SQ4.1: Reliability: Flaky tests reduce the reliability of testing.
developers rate issues in setup and teardown to be the most common causes of flaky tests.
